source.title: P-MMEval: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Consistent Evaluation of LLMs
source.authors: Yi-Dan Zhang; Yunyang Wan; Bo-Yi Deng; Bao-Song Yang; Hao-Ran Wei; Fei Huang; Bo-Wen Yu; Dayiheng Liu; Jun-Yang Lin; Jing-Ren Zhou

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table content is flattened in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Compares multilingual downstream task performance across model sizes, but does not measure pretraining loss or fit power laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-size-related downstream scores and trends relevant to V6. It does not test held-out cross-entropy scaling, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or architecture variation at fixed size. Prompt comparisons and cross-language accuracy consistency ratios are not results about size-dependent downstream performance as named in V6.
record.test_reason: A multilingual benchmark paper that incidentally compares off-the-shelf instruction-tuned models of different sizes within the same families (Qwen2.5 0.5B–72B, LLaMA3.x, Gemma2, Aya, Mistral). Its Table 3 scores bear qualitatively on V6, whether downstream performance improves with scale, in a new multilingual setting. It fits no curve, does not use pretraining loss, and models within a family are not controlled for data or recipe, so this is a weak, descriptive test of V6 only.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors present a parallel multilingual benchmark and report that larger models are generally more capable (citing Kaplan), with strong gains on understanding and reasoning tasks but only slight gains on generation and a LLaMA3.2 exception. Their main emphases are prompt effects, language differences, benchmark-origin sensitivity, and cross-lingual transfer, where code transfers easiest and logical reasoning hardest.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates task accuracy and related benchmark scores across existing instruction-tuned models; it does not train model-size sweeps or fit held-out loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports benchmark sensitivity to prompt choice and benchmark origin; model-size trends also vary by task and model series.

fits_no_version.finding: The cross-lingual accuracy consistency ratio (CACR, English→target) generally rises with size for Gemma2, LLaMA3.1 and Mistral, while Qwen2.5 shows saturation on some tasks (Section 5.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-lingual transfer consistency improves with model size, but saturates in some model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Arabic performance of ~7B models is near the bottom but improves to mid-low at 14B and above (Section 4.5, Fig. 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scale gains on downstream tasks differ by language.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2024
record.problems: The evidence concerns downstream task scores rather than held-out loss; the paper gives no fitted scaling curves, uncertainty estimates, or predictive tests. Some reported trends are qualitative, and the task metrics differ.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 contains many per-model, per-task scores; these were not exhaustively transcribed because the version tested is the broad size-related downstream-performance claim and the table is flattened in the supplied text. Prompt comparisons in Table 4 and CACR results in Sections 5 and Appendix E were left out because they do not directly measure downstream task performance as a function of model size for V6.

untested.parts: Predictability: no fitted functional form, no extrapolation, and no link to pretraining loss. Scale is parameter count of differently trained released models, not controlled compute.

missing.what: Per-series AVG_S/AVG_U trends as read from the flattened table: Qwen2.5 AVG_S 24.42, 41.06, 56.45, 65.28, 69.20, 71.95, 73.13 (0.5B–72B); Gemma2 AVG_S 45.69, 64.23, 68.64; LLaMA3.1 AVG_S 56.03→70.02; Aya AVG_S 49.08→61.83
COMET scores clustered at 80–89 with negligible differences across large size gaps
HumanEval-XL JavaScript/Java pass@1 rises with size, e.g. Qwen2.5 JS 14.25 (0.5B) to 75.00 (72B)

record.verdict_notes: Table 3 is flattened, so the column mapping above was reconstructed and should be checked against the PDF; FLORES values were cross-checked against Table 5. Size comparisons mix in a prompt change (direct answering below 7B, CoT for MGSM at 7B and above) and come from separately trained released models, so this is weak evidence for V6. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No relationship to pretraining loss, predictive fit, or extrapolation to much larger runs is tested.

rows.subject: Representative multilingual model series (aggregate statement)
rows.size_stated: various model sizes; specific range not stated
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated downstream benchmark performance across model sizes.

conditions.value: standard EN prompt except where otherwise specified

rows.measure: Benchmark task performance; metric varies by task
rows.value: The authors report generally stronger multilingual capabilities with increasing model size, with significant improvement on understanding and capability-specialized tasks.
rows.note: This is the authors' aggregate qualitative description of results across model series and tasks, not a fitted scaling relationship.
rows.check: Qualitative aggregate statement. It is supported by Table 3 series averages, which no row records (see missing).

rows.subject: LLaMA3.2-3B
rows.operation_detail: Compared performance with the smaller LLaMA3.2-1B model.

conditions.value: multilingual tasks; specific aggregate measure not stated

rows.note: The authors attribute the decline to poor instruction-following and increased answer-extraction failure in both small LLaMA3.2 models.
rows.check: The decline is small (Table 3 as flattened: AVG_S 28.03→27.29, AVG_U 28.08→27.21), and FLORES BLEU rises 29.30→36.85. The authors attribute the dip to answer-extraction failures rather than capability, so this is a weak reversal on a measurement artifact.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, lines 873–879; Table 3: AVG_S 28.03→27.29 and AVG_U 28.08→27.21.

rows.subject: QWEN 2.5-0.5B
rows.operation_detail: Measured MGSM performance as part of the QWEN 2.5 size series.
rows.note: The paper gives this score as the smaller endpoint of its QWEN 2.5 MGSM comparison; the score alone does not establish a scaling effect.
rows.check: This is only the baseline endpoint of R4, not a separate result; merge it into R4. The condition is also wrong: the paper says models under 7B use direct answering rather than CoT, so Qwen2.5-0.5B's MGSM score was not obtained under CoT.

source_check.correct: Qwen2.5-0.5B MGSM accuracy: 13.12; direct-answering prompt, not CoT. Models below 7B use direct answering because CoT increases answer-extraction failures.
source_check.problem: The prompting condition is wrong; this endpoint also duplicates the baseline of R4.

rows.subject: QWEN 2.5-72B
rows.operation_detail: Compared MGSM performance with the 0.5B model in the QWEN 2.5 series.
rows.note: The paper states these are the scores for the 0.5B and 72B models, respectively.
rows.check: Condition 'prompt: CoT' applies only to the 72B endpoint. The 0.5B baseline used direct answering (Section 4.2), so the 13.12→91.00 gap mixes scale with a prompting change.

source_check.correct: MGSM accuracy: Qwen2.5-0.5B, direct answering, 13.12; Qwen2.5-72B, CoT, 91.00. Standard EN instructions apply.
source_check.problem: CoT applies only to the larger endpoint; the comparison changes prompting as well as model size.

rows.subject: Evaluated models (aggregate statement)
rows.size_stated: various model sizes; specific range not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared generation-task performance across model sizes.
rows.value: The paper reports slight improvement with size and says generation performance does not improve proportionally.
rows.note: The text does not assign this qualitative finding to a specific model or give a fitted trend.
rows.check: The aggregate wording hides series differences. Qwen2.5 BLEU rises 15.95 (0.5B) to 41.55 (72B), Gemma2 rises 24.00 to 42.23, but LLaMA3.1 is flat at 16.59 (8B) vs 16.63 (70B). COMET differences are described as negligible (Appendix B).

source_check.problem: The qualitative wording matches the authors, but aggregates substantial series differences: Qwen2.5 BLEU 15.95→41.55, Gemma2 24.00→42.23, and LLaMA3.1 16.59→16.63.

relationships.condition: Understanding and capability-specialized task averages within model families (Qwen2.5, Gemma2, LLaMA3.1, Mistral, Aya)
relationships.reason: Scores rise with size, e.g. Qwen2.5 MGSM 13.12→91.00 and, by flattened Table 3, AVG_S rising across sizes 24.42→73.13 (R1, R4; series averages are in missing).
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased with size, including Qwen2.5 MGSM from 13.12 to 91.00 and its specialized-task average from 24.42 to 73.13.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Understanding and capability-specialized task averages within model families (Qwen2.5, Gemma2, LLaMA3.1, Mistral, Aya)
source_check.reason: R1 and Table 3 support generally improving task averages with size in these families. R4's MGSM endpoints are correct, but use different prompting methods. Support is qualitative; predictive accuracy and pretraining-loss relationships remain untested.

relationships.reason: Scores dip slightly from 1B to 3B; the authors attribute this to answer-extraction failures, and they call sub-7B results highly variable and prompt-sensitive (R2).
relationships.display_finding: LLaMA3.2 scores fell from 28.03 to 27.29 on AVG_S and 28.08 to 27.21 on AVG_U, attributed to answer-extraction failures; broader sub-7B results were highly variable and prompt-sensitive.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R2 explicitly reports reversal for LLaMA3.2: AVG_S 28.03→27.29 and AVG_U 28.08→27.21. Under the verdict rules this condition challenges improvement with scale, even with the authors' extraction-failure explanation. Separate the broader sub-7B prompt-sensitivity qualification; it does not establish reversal for all small models.

relationships.reason: Gains are slight and non-proportional; LLaMA3.1 BLEU stays at 16.59→16.63 from 8B to 70B, and COMET barely differs across sizes (R5; LLaMA3.1 values in missing).
relationships.display_finding: LLaMA3.1 BLEU barely changed from 16.59 to 16.63 between 8B and 70B, while Qwen2.5 and Gemma2 improved substantially; COMET varied little, attributed to insufficient metric discrimination.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R5 supports a qualified aggregate description, but the condition combines different outcomes and needs splitting: Qwen2.5 and Gemma2 BLEU improve substantially, while LLaMA3.1 is nearly flat at 16.59→16.63. COMET clustering is attributed to insufficient metric discrimination, not demonstrated absence of capability gains. Non-proportional improvement alone does not contradict V6, which specifies no proportionality.
